i < numNodes * numNodes; ++i) {\n        dist[i] = rangeMin + (unsigned int)(range * rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX);\n    }\n    \n    // Set diagonal to zero (distance from node to itself is 0)\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n        dist[idx2(i, i, numNodes)] = 0;\n    }\n}\n\nvoid initializePathMatrix(std::vector<unsigned int>& path, const size_t numNodes) {\n    for (size_t j = 0; j < numNodes; ++j) {\n        for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n            path[idx2(i, j, numNodes)] = j;\n            path[idx2(j, i, numNodes)] = i;\n        }\n        path[idx2(j, j, numNodes)] = j;\n    }\n}\n\nvoid floydWarshall(std::vector<unsigned int>& dist, \n                   std::vector<unsigned int>& path, \n                   const size_t numNodes) {\n    // Classic Floyd-Warshall algorithm\n    // For each intermediate node k\n    for (size_t k = 0; k < numNodes; ++k) {\n        // For each source node i\n        for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n            // For each destination node j\n            for (size_t j = 0; j < numNodes; ++j) {\n                const unsigned int distIJ = dist[idx2(j, i, numNodes)];\n                const unsigned int distIK = dist[idx2(k, i, numNodes)];\n                const unsigned int distKJ = dist[idx2(j, k, numNodes)];\n                \n                const unsigned int newDist = distIK + distKJ;\n                \n                if (newDist < distIJ) {\n                    dist[idx2(j, i, numNodes)] = newDist;\n                    path[idx2(j, i, numNodes)] = k;\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\nbool validateResult(const std::vector<unsigned int>& dist, const size_t numNodes) {\n    // Basic sanity checks\n    \n    // 1. {\n        for (size_t j = 0; j < std::min(numNodes, static_cast<size_t>(10)); ++j) {\n            for (size_t k = 0; k < numNodes; ++k) {\n                const unsigned int distIJ = dist[idx2(j, i, I also verify the invariant row/column k: since M[k][k]=0, updates to M[k][y] and M[x][k] during the k-th iteration never strictly decrease, so the in-place algorithm stays correct without needing separate buffers.\n\nI'm also checking overflow safety — since edge weights are capped and n is bounded, summed distances never realistically exceed what fits in the integer type, and INF is unused here so there's no special wraparound to worry about.\n\nNow I'm sketching the parallel design: a 2D process grid for MPI where each phase k requires broadcasting the pivot row and column segments across the grid, with communication cost roughly O(n/P + n/Q) per iteration.\n\nI'm defining each rank's ownership of row and column blocks, then for each phase k, broadcasting column k's values along row communicators and row k's values along column communicators from the ranks that own them, so every process can locally apply the min-plus update.\n\nI'm double-checking that the pivot cell itself stays invariant during its own phase, confirming that broadcast timing relative to the local update doesn't matter. I'm also noting pipelining/lookahead of the next pivot row/column as a possible performance optimization to overlap communication with compute, though that adds complexity.\n\nFor the simple blocking design, I'm estimating overhead: per phase k there are two broadcasts, and for small n (like 512 with 4 ranks) the latency from hundreds of iterations could dominate over the trivial GPU compute cost. This suggests switching to blocked Floyd-Warshall with block size B, broadcasting B rows/columns together and processing phases locally to cut down the synchronization count.\n\nI'm thinking through the classic three-phase blocked FW: the diagonal block owner computes FW on its B×B block first, broadcasts it to row and column panel owners, those update their panels, broadcast again, and then all remaining blocks get updated using the row and column panels—trading implementation complexity for far fewer communication rounds.\n\nI'm also checking correctness: since shortest-path distances are unique minima, the blocked algorithm converges to the exact same final distance matrix as naive order-k FW, even though intermediate values differ along the way. A cleaner hybrid might just use MPI across nodes with CUDA as the primary compute engine, reserving OpenMP for simpler host-side tasks rather than splitting the main computation between CPU and GPU.\n\nI'm now weighing a simpler design where the GPU does essentially all the compute per phase, and OpenMP handles only host-side parallel work like initialization, packing/unpacking buffers, validation, and hashing results. The catch is that the rand_r-based initialization is inherently sequential, so parallelizing it would require tricky jump-ahead math on the LCG state that doesn't seem worth the effort -- so I'm settling on keeping that part sequential and focusing OpenMP's role on the other host tasks.\n\nFor the MPI/CUDA split, I'm thinking through a 2D process grid with block distribution, where each rank keeps its local block on device memory and runs a kernel per phase to update it. Pivot extraction matters here: in column-major storage, pulling a pivot column is a contiguous memory slice, but pulling a pivot row is strided, so I'd need either a gather kernel or cudaMemcpy2D to pack it efficiently before broadcasting, while keeping in mind the final hash just reflects the array in its original storage order.\n\nEstimating memory traffic for the naive full-sweep kernel on large n, the workload is clearly memory-bound rather than compute-bound — roughly 8-9 seconds per GPU at typical bandwidth for n=16384 split across 4 GPUs — versus a blocked/shared-memory tiled approach that could become compute-bound instead, running much faster due to high integer throughput.\n\nI'm now working through whether a tiled kernel can still reproduce the exact naive phase-by-phase update order: for a tile (I,J) away from the pivot tile K, I need the intermediate values of row/column tiles (I,K) and (K,J) at each phase k within the block, since those tiles themselves get updated internally as k sweeps through K before being used to update (I,J).\n\nI'm questioning whether using the fully-updated diagonal tile at block end, rather than its intermediate per-phase snapshot, still gives correct results for the (I,K) tile update — checking if that discrepancy actually matters given row invariance within a phase.\n\nSo the resolution seems to be: I need to snapshot the pivot row of the diagonal tile at each internal phase, since the in-place diagonal update changes that row before the (I,K) tile can use it. That means storing B snapshot vectors (one per phase) per block, which captures exactly what each off-diagonal tile needs during that phase.\n\nFor off-diagonal tiles (I,J), each phase k' pulls a recorded pivot column from (I,K) and a recorded pivot row from (K,J) at the state before phase k' updates them, letting the tile sweep through all B phases exactly as naive Floyd-Warshall would, just restricted to block-local shared memory and recorded vectors.\n\n3. The column panel update within phase k' stays in-place since column k' is invariant during that phase, and the row k' values it depends on come from the diag tile's recorded state at phase k'-1, which also stays fixed throughout phase k'.\n\nExtending this symmetrically, the row panel (K,J) updates the same way using recorded column values, and finally the off-diagonal tile (I,J) combines the recorded column values from panel (I,K) with the recorded row values from panel (K,J) at each phase k' to compute its minimum.\n\nSince blocks are processed in order K=0,1,... and within each block phases k' proceed sequentially, the global order of updates for every element matches increasing k, matching the naive algorithm exactly.\n\nThis maps to classic distributed blocked Floyd-Warshall: for each of the n/B blocks K, the owner of the diagonal tile (K,K) computes the diagonal update step first and broadcasts the resulting row/column data needed for dependent tiles.\n\nWith a 2D block-cyclic distribution across a P×Q process grid, the diagonal tile gets broadcast to all ranks, while the updated column panel for block K is broadcast along process rows so that every rank holding tiles in that row range can proceed with its local updates.\n\nBut I realize I need to be careful: the column value at index k' isn't fixed once computed—later phases (k'' > k') can still modify column k' in a tile, since column k' updates whenever it's beaten by col_{k''}[x] + row_{k''}[k']. So I actually need to snapshot the state of column k' specifically at the moment phase k' executes, not just rely on the final value, which means I need per-phase recording of that column.\n\nFor the column panel update, D(k',k) comes from the diag tile row at the start of phase k', which stays fixed throughout that phase — so I need to snapshot both rowDiag[k'] and colDiag[k'] (each B values) per phase to broadcast separately.\n\nActually this simplifies nicely: for each global phase k', naive FW just needs the full pivot row and column at that moment, which is exactly colk'[x] = D(x,k') and rowk'[y] = D(k',y). So blocking is really just a reordering of these same phase-by-phase updates across tiles rather than a fundamentally different computation.\n\nI can precompute, for each block of B phases, all the pivot vectors pivotCol[k'][x] and pivotRow[k'][y] up front — just 2Bn values — then apply the same naive update rule fused across those B phases for every tile. Each tile (I,J) only needs the slices of those pivot vectors matching its row and column range, which means the in-block computation of these pivots requires correctly solving the sequential sub-Floyd-Warshall over the diagonal and panel tiles first.\n\nSo the blocked approach is just running the naive phase sequentially within the block itself: for each k' in the block, compute the pivot column/row using only panel updates from earlier phases, update the panel for phase k', then defer updating the rest of the matrix until the whole block's pivots are ready.\n\nEstimating the communication cost: broadcasting pivot columns and rows across all blocks amounts to roughly 2n² integers total over the run, which for n=16384 is around 2GB per rank — fast enough on a good fabric relative to compute time, though I'm considering restricting broadcasts to only the ranks that actually need each pivot segment to cut this down further.\n\nNow I'm settling on a 2D block-cyclic tile distribution with tile size B, where tile (I,J) is owned by rank (I mod P, J mod Q), and working out how the sequential dependency chain within a panel update requires each step's pivot column to be fully available across all row ranks before proceeding.\n\nSo the dependency chain resolves to: the diagonal tile must finish its own internal Floyd-Warshall phases first since it needs its own column, and only after that can the column panel tiles proceed, each requiring the diagonal tile's snapshots at every phase.\n\nOnce I have those snapshots, column panel tiles across all I can be processed independently and in-order internally, and the same logic applies symmetrically to row panel tiles across all J. Off-diagonal tiles then depend only on the already-computed column and row panel snapshots, giving a clean one-to-one dependency structure per tile, so I'm laying out the per-block algorithm: first the diagonal owner runs its in-tile FW to produce row and column snapshots at each phase, then broadcasts those snapshot values to the ranks that need them.\n\nSince diagRow[k'][k']=0, the diagonal entry is trivially correct regardless of ordering, and column k' stays invariant through phase k'. Once S2 finishes, each column-tile owner holds snapshots colSnap[k'][x] for x in I, k' in K — a B² block per tile I — which then get broadcast to the other ranks sharing that process row.\n\nThese broadcasts can be aggregated per process row rather than done tile-by-tile: the root rank for that row (holding column K mod Q) packs all its row's colSnap tiles into one buffer and broadcasts over the row communicator, sized by the number of tiles times B². By symmetry, S3 handles the row panel tiles the same way, with rowSnap[k'][y] snapshots for y in J owned by ranks at (K mod P, J mod Q).\n\nFor S4, I work out that off-diagonal tile updates D(x,y) via D(x,k')+D(k',y) using the precomputed colSnap and rowSnap, and since these snapshots don't depend on the evolving tile, the inner loop over k' in the block is essentially just a min-plus matrix product over a B-sized contraction dimension.\n\nFor path tracking, I process k' ascending and only update the predecessor when a strictly smaller candidate distance is found, which matches the naive sequential algorithm's tie-breaking rule and doesn't require any extra communication since the index k' is already known locally. Dependencies flow S1 to S2/S3 (needing the broadcasted diagonal snapshot) then to S4 (needing colSnap/rowSnap broadcasts), and I'm now tallying the communication cost per block.\n\nThinking through the pipeline's concurrency: S1 is a small serial step on the diagonal owner, but S2 and S3 only run on the subset of ranks in the relevant process row/column, leaving other ranks idle while the bulk S4 work happens elsewhere. I'm considering whether idle ranks could start on next block's S4 work early, and whether lookahead pipelining lets the following block's S1 begin as soon as its diagonal tile is finalized by the current block's S4, rather than waiting for the whole block to complete.\n\nGiven the goal of maximum performance, I'm leaning toward keeping the algorithm synchronous per block but pushing the bulk S4 computation onto GPU kernels, launched once per block across all blocks, since the panel work S1-S3 is comparatively tiny and could instead run on the CPU via OpenMP threads over tiles while the GPU handles S4 in parallel.\n\nThe catch is data movement: since MPI broadcasts need host-resident buffers regardless of CUDA-aware support, I'll need D2H/H2D staging transfers every block for the panel and diagonal tiles, but back-of-envelope math suggests the total transfer volume stays well under a second even for large n, with per-block sync overhead adding up to tens of milliseconds at worst — acceptable for large problem sizes and trivial for small ones.\n\nKeeping the matrix entirely on host and shuttling full tiles to the GPU every block would mean moving n² data per block, which is way too costly — the matrix really needs to live device-resident. So the simplest sound design keeps local tiles on GPU, computes the panel there with a kernel, and only extracts the snapshot needed for MPI exchange onto the host.\n\nI'm estimating launch overhead: one kernel per phase per panel would mean tens of thousands of launches across the full run, costing noticeable time at large n. Instead, a single kernel per panel that loops over all B phases internally, using one CUDA block per tile with __syncthreads between phases, avoids that overhead since each phase only depends on the tile itself plus the diagonal snapshot already in memory.\n\nNow I'm working out how the diagonal snapshots move between devices: after the owner computes S1 in a single-block kernel, it needs to copy the diagonal row and column snapshots (each B×B) to host, broadcast via MPI, then copy back to device memory on all ranks before launching S2/S3/S4, since those kernels reference the snapshot values rather than the live diagonal tile.\n\nThen I need to exchange these snapshots: after computing them for owned panel tiles, D2H and broadcast colSnap along the row communicator and rowSnap along the column communicator, so each rank ends up with the snapshots needed for its local tiles. I'm thinking through how to balance tile counts per process row evenly, possibly padding n so every rank holds the same number of tiles.\n\nOn padding, I'm checking that padded vertices stay safe: since their distances start at INF (except the diagonal), any path routed through a padded vertex sums to at least INF, which can never beat a real shortest path bounded by roughly 200·n. So padding doesn't corrupt real distances, and I'm confirming the padded entries themselves can't spuriously drop below INF either, since they'd require summing two INF-tier values which stays above the real-value range.\n\nChecking the sums confirm no value ever exceeds INF since nothing gets updated beyond that bound, so padded pivots never corrupt real entries, and since their own values aren't part of the output, the extra computation is safely irrelevant.\n\nPadded entries can be affected by real phases but they never feed back into real-to-real computations since those only ever pivot through real indices — so skipping padded phases entirely is safe and correct.\n\nIt's irrelevant anyway since padded entries never factor into real results, so initializing them as INF with zero diagonal is fine either way. Instead of padding to a multiple of B×P×Q, I should think about a simpler padding scheme.\n\nLet me define NB as the number of tile rows/cols after padding n to a multiple of B, then use a block-cyclic distribution across a P×Q process grid where tile ownership naturally handles NB not being an exact multiple of P or Q. I'll use MPI_Dims_create to pick P×Q, and the block-cyclic scheme should handle uneven tile counts per process row without special-casing.\n\nFor stage S4, each process runs a kernel over its owned off-diagonal tiles (I,J) where I≠K and J≠K, skipping panel tiles. The colSnap for tile (I,K) is owned by rank (I mod P, K mod Q) and broadcast along that process row so every rank owning row I gets it, and similarly rowSnap is broadcast along process columns -- the panel tiles themselves were already correctly updated in S2 and don't need further S4 updates.\n\nEstimating synchronous overhead per block (D2H/H2D transfers, broadcasts, kernel launches each requiring a sync point) at roughly 6 sync points of ~50μs each, for n=16384 with NB=256 blocks that's about 80ms overhead against ~1.1s of compute time, so around 7% -- acceptable, and negligible for smaller n. I consider overlapping communication with S4 via lookahead on the next block's panel tiles but decide to keep the implementation straightforward and synchronous for now, noting overlap as a possible future optimization.\n\nNow I'm thinking through where OpenMP parallelism fits in -- particularly host-side initialization of the matrix. Since rand_r calls are inherently sequential over the flat index, generating n² values per rank could take 1-2 seconds for n=16384, which rivals the actual compute time and would hurt scalability. I consider whether rand_r's internal state transition allows jump-ahead so I can parallelize generation in chunks, and start recalling the glibc implementation details of rand_r to see if its linear congruential-style update can be mathematically advanced without computing every intermediate step.\n\nI work through the affine structure of rand_r's state updates, concluding that jump-ahead is theoretically possible in logarithmic time since each call composes a few LCG steps, but implementing this would mean reimplementing libc's rand_r, risking divergence if the platform's implementation differs. Given that risk, I lean toward just accepting the sequential O(n²) generation cost per rank, estimating it at around 1.5 seconds compared to similar compute time.\n\nThen I realize the key insight: the original code's timed region excludes initialization entirely, only measuring the Floyd-Warshall computation itself, so this generation cost doesn't even matter for fair comparison. That means I just need each rank to independently generate the full matrix (no communication needed since it's deterministic) and store only its local tiles, accepting the redundant per-rank computation as a non-bottleneck since it runs concurrently and I can't easily parallelize a sequential stream anyway.\n\nFor OpenMP, I'm now weighing whether to use it meaningfully on host-side operations like packing/unpacking snapshot buffers, versus doing the CPU-side panel work (S1-S3) with threads -- though that would require costly device-to-host roundtrips each block, whereas keeping those as GPU kernels avoids that latency.\n\nThis points to a classic lookahead approach — letting the GPU prioritize panel-relevant tiles first so the CPU can start panel work while the rest finishes on device. But before designing further, I should check whether the environment actually has CUDA, MPI, and a GPU available, since that fundamentally changes what's feasible to implement and test.\n\n","time":{"start":1793140720395,"end":1793140861575},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

Writing kernel template...\n\nWriting kernel argument setup...\n\nMapping out the DIAG case needing its own kernel since it writes both row and column snapshots into separate halves of the output buffer, unlike COL/ROW which write to a single offset.\n\nWriting update kernel code...\n\nWriting kernel update loop...\n\nWriting the panel kernel...\n\nFor ROW, the base index works out so blockStride is T² and tileOff scales with lkRow*NLJ*T², confirming the offsets check out for both column and row cases. Now I'm working out the global index strides for COL and ROW modes, making sure the skip condition triggers correctly when g equals K, then moving into writing the kernel body with shared memory buffers for the data and predicate tiles.\n\nWriting shared memory load logic...\n\nWriting update logic...\n\nI'm snapshotting the appropriate row/column values for each case, then updating the distance matrix for the 32x32 tile using pivot row and column values, checking synchronization points to ensure pc/pr are loaded before use—two syncs per phase.\n\nChecking the thread guard condition against block dimensions, and confirming shared memory usage for sD, sP, and the pc/pr arrays stays comfortably under the 48KB limit. Now I'm looking at how the host-side distance arrays are laid out per tile.\n\nI need to allocate the full local arrays on the device sized by NLI*NLJ*T² elements, then gather results back by copying device memory to a pinned host buffer before using MPI_Gatherv to collect everything. I'm also working out the serial initialization function for the local tiles, including the random seed and range calculations used to generate distance values.\n\nFor ownership, I'm computing which rank owns each (x,y) pair based on tile indices, storing values at the correct offset in the local distance buffer, then handling boundary cases: diagonal entries get zero, and padding entries beyond the actual node count get set to infinity unless they're on the diagonal.\n\nSo padded diagonal entries get zeroed during the fill pass, while the stream pass never touches padding—so the overwrite order works out correctly. Path indexing for each local tile uses the global y-coordinate computed from tile and local offsets, applying consistently to padded elements too.\n\nI'm parallelizing the tile loops with OpenMP, using the default thread count, and applying the same parallel unpacking approach to the gather step across ranks' tiles. The program prints the computation time, then rank 0 alone performs validation against the full distance matrix and determines the exit code while other ranks simply return 0—relying on MPI's exit status handling to propagate rank 0's result; only rank 0 prints validation output.\n\nNow I'm sketching out the main function: initializing MPI, getting rank/size, parsing arguments identically on all ranks, and handling help/unknown-option cases where only rank 0 prints before finalizing and returning. Printing elsewhere is also gated to rank 0 only. After that, I set up the process grid (P, Q, row/col communicators), assign GPUs per rank, compute tile dimensions, allocate pinned host and device memory, initialize the graph data across ranks, transfer to device, then run the Floyd-Warshall computation wrapped in barriers and timers to measure total elapsed time.\n\nI'm also working through edge cases: n=0 should degenerate gracefully with zero-sized allocations and empty kernel loops, while negative n (via atoi) would produce a huge size_t that triggers a CUDA allocation failure caught by the error-checking macro, which aborts via MPI_Abort. I'm also deciding to keep tile counts and indices as int while using size_t for byte offsets, since even large problem sizes split across a 2D process grid keep per-rank tile counts well within int range.\n\nFor the gather step at large n, the total element count could overflow a 32-bit count or displacement, so I'm avoiding a single MPI_Gatherv and instead having rank 0 serially receive each rank's packed buffer with individual Send/Recv pairs, unpacking directly into the output array -- this sidesteps the overflow risk since each rank's count individually stays under the int limit, and it's only used for the optional validation/print path anyway.\n\nNow I'm planning the final file: parallelizing the unpack step with OpenMP, broadcasting pinned host buffers for the device, and cleaning up dead code like the old host-side Floyd-Warshall implementation and unused helper functions that would otherwise clutter the build.\n\nI'm setting up the CMake build to compile the executable as CUDA with CXX and MPI dependencies, configuring architectures and standards, and preparing compile options for the target.\n\nThere's a concern about whether nvcc properly handles the OpenMP compile flag when linked through the OpenMP interface target—nvcc typically needs `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` rather than a raw `-fopenmp` flag, so I'm considering writing explicit CUDA-specific compile flags rather than relying on CMake's propagation from OpenMP::OpenMP_CXX.\n\nThere's also a real risk that the system's nvcc (CUDA 12.0) won't support GCC 13, since that combination is known to fail without an unsupported-compiler flag. {"type":"tool_use","timestamp":1793141210925,"sessionID":"ses_e807c23a9ffecLzhcZkkw485d1","part":{"type":"tool","tool":"write","callID":"toolu_01DzzJL2MphxZ2TnvWU47rBV","state":{"status":"completed","input":{"filePath":"/home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/floydwarshall_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_hybrid_r5/floydwarshall/floydwarshall.cpp","content":"// Hybrid MPI + OpenMP + CUDA Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path benchmark.\n//\n// Decomposition\n//   * MPI:    the NB x NB grid of TILE x TILE tiles is distributed block-cyclically\n//             over a P x Q process grid. Tile (I,J) belongs to rank (I%P, J%Q).\n//             Each rank drives one GPU (local rank modulo device count).\n//   * CUDA:   blocked Floyd-Warshall. For each block index K, the pivot tile (K,K)\n//             is processed first, then the row/column panels (K,J)/(I,K), and finally\n//             every remaining tile (I,J) is relaxed with all TILE pivots of block K\n//             fused in registers.\n//   * OpenMP: host-side data-parallel loops (tile initialization, result gathering).\n//\n// Equivalence with the sequential k-outer algorithm\n//   Within block K the pivot phases are replayed in ascending k order. For every\n//   phase k the pivot column D(.,k) and pivot row D(k,.) are captured exactly as they\n//   are at the start of that phase (snapshots), so each element receives the same\n//   sequence of relaxations as in the original code. Distances and path entries\n//   (including tie-breaking, since updates are strict '<') are therefore identical.\n//   Padding (n rounded up to a multiple of TILE) only adds INF rows/columns whose\n//   pivot phases are skipped, so they never influence real entries.\n\n#include <mpi.h>\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include <cuda_runtime.h>\n\n#include \"../common/results_output.hpp\"\n\nconstexpr unsigned int INF = 1000000000;\nconstexpr unsigned int MAX_DISTANCE = 200;\n\nconstexpr int TILE = 64;           // tile edge length (phases fused per block)\nconstexpr int TT = TILE * TILE;    // elements per tile\nconstexpr int THREADS = 256;       // 16 x 16 threads per CUDA block\nconstexpr int RPT = TILE / 16;     // elements per thread per dimension\nstatic_assert(RPT * 16 == TILE, \"TILE must be a multiple of 16\");\n\n#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                              \\\n    do {                                                                              \\\n        cudaError_t err_ = (call);                                                    \\\n        if (err_ != cudaSuccess) {                                                    \\\n            fprintf(stderr, \"CUDA error '%s' at %s:%d: %s\\n\", cudaGetErrorString(err_), \\\n                    __FILE__, __LINE__, #call);                                       \\\n            MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);                                             \\\n        }                                                                             \\\n    } while (0)\n\n// Index calculation for flattened 2D array\ninline constexpr size_t idx2(const size_t i, const size_t j, const size_t n) noexcept {\n    return j * n + i;\n}\n\n// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n// Device kernels\n// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nenum PanelMode { PANEL_DIAG = 0, PANEL_COL = 1, PANEL_ROW = 2 };\n\n// Processes the pivot phases of block K inside one tile per CUDA block.\n//   PANEL_DIAG: tile (K,K). Updated in place; snapOut receives\n//               diagRow[kp][y] = D(K.kp, K.y) and diagCol[kp][x] = D(K.x, K.kp)\n//               (values at the start of phase kp).\n//   PANEL_COL:  tile (I,K), I != K. Pivot row comes from diag snapshot piv;\n//               snapOut receives colSnap[kp][x] = D(I.x, K.kp) at phase kp start.\n//   PANEL_ROW:  tile (K,J), J != K. Pivot column comes from diag snapshot piv;\n//               snapOut receives rowSnap[kp][y] = D(K.kp, J.y) at phase kp start.\n// Block b of the grid addresses tile gDist + b*blockStride; for COL/ROW blocks\n// are the local tile rows/columns, and gStart/gStep map block b to the global index.\ntemplate <int MODE>\n__global__ void __launch_bounds__(THREADS)\npanelKernel(unsigned int* __restrict__ gDist, unsigned int* __restrict__ gPath,\n            const size_t blockStride, const int gStart, const int gStep, const int K,\n            const int kBase, const int kmax, const unsigned int* __restrict__ piv,\n            unsigned int* __restrict__ snapOut) {\n    if (MODE != PANEL_DIAG && gStart + static_cast<int>(blockIdx.x) * gStep == K) {\n        return;  // the pivot tile itself is handled by PANEL_DIAG\n    }\n\n    unsigned int* D = gDist + static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * blockStride;\n    unsigned int* P = gPath + static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * blockStride;\n    unsigned int* S = snapOut + static_cast<size_t>(blockIdx.x) * TT;\n\n    __shared__ unsigned int sD[TT];   // distances, storage index yl*TILE + xl\n    __shared__ unsigned int sP[TT];   // path\n    __shared__ unsigned int pc[TILE]; // pivot column for the current phase\n    __shared__ unsigned int pr[TILE]; // pivot row for the current phase\n\n    const int tid = threadIdx.x;\n    const int tx = tid & 15;\n    const int ty = tid >> 4;\n\n    for (int t = tid; t < TT; t += THREADS) {\n        sD[t] = D[t];\n        sP[t] = P[t];\n    }\n    __syncthreads();\n\n    for (int kp = 0; kp < kmax; ++kp) {\n        __syncthreads();  // previous phase fully applied\n        if (tid < TILE) {\n            if (MODE == PANEL_DIAG) {\n                pc[tid] = sD[kp * TILE + tid];   // D(x=tid, kp)\n                pr[tid] = sD[tid * TILE + kp];   // D(kp, y=tid)\n            } else if (MODE == PANEL_COL) {\n                pc[tid] = sD[kp * TILE + tid];   // D(x=tid, kp), local column kp\n                pr[tid] = piv[kp * TILE + tid];  // diagRow[kp][y]\n            } else {\n                pr[tid] = sD[tid * TILE + kp];   // D(kp, y=tid), local row kp\n                pc[tid] = piv[kp * TILE + tid];  // diagCol[kp][x]\n            }\n        }\n        __syncthreads();\n\n        if (tid < TILE) {\n            if (MODE == PANEL_DIAG) {\n                S[kp * TILE + tid] = pr[tid];\n                S[TT + kp * TILE + tid] = pc[tid];\n            } else if (MODE == PANEL_COL) {\n                S[kp * TILE + tid] = pc[tid];\n            } else {\n                S[kp * TILE + tid] = pr[tid];\n            }\n        }\n\n        const unsigned int kg = static_cast<unsigned int>(kBase + kp);\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int a = 0; a < RPT; ++a) {\n#pragma unroll\n            for (int b = 0; b < RPT; ++b) {\n                const int x = tx + 16 * a;\n                const int y = ty + 16 * b;\n                const int idx = y * TILE + x;\n                const unsigned int nd = pc[x] + pr[y];\n                if (nd < sD[idx]) {\n                    sD[idx] = nd;\n                    sP[idx] = kg;\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    __syncthreads();\n\n    for (int t = tid; t < TT; t += THREADS) {\n        D[t] = sD[t];\n        P[t] = sP[t];\n    }\n}\n\n// Relaxes every tile (I,J) with I != K and J != K using all kmax pivots of block K.\n// Grid: (NLJ, NLI) local tiles.\n__global__ void __launch_bounds__(THREADS)\nupdateKernel(unsigned int* __restrict__ gDist, unsigned int* __restrict__ gPath,\n             const int NLJ, const int r, const int c, const int P, const int Q, const int K,\n             const int kBase, const int kmax,\n             const unsigned int* __restrict__ colSnap,\n             const unsigned int* __restrict__ rowSnap) {\n    const int lj = blockIdx.x;\n    const int li = blockIdx.y;\n    const int I = r + li * P;\n    const int J = c + lj * Q;\n    if (I == K || J == K) return;\n\n    __shared__ unsigned int sCol[TT];  // sCol[kp*TILE + x] = D(I.x, K.kp)\n    __shared__ unsigned int sRow[TT];  // sRow[kp*TILE + y] = D(K.kp, J.y)\n\n    const int tid = threadIdx.x;\n    const int tx = tid & 15;\n    const int ty = tid >> 4;\n\n    const unsigned int* cs = colSnap + static_cast<size_t>(li) * TT;\n    const unsigned int* rs = rowSnap + static_cast<size_t>(lj) * TT;\n    for (int t = tid; t < kmax * TILE; t += THREADS) {\n        sCol[t] = cs[t];\n        sRow[t] = rs[t];\n    }\n\n    const size_t base = (static_cast<size_t>(li) * NLJ + lj) * TT;\n    unsigned int* D = gDist + base;\n    unsigned int* Pa = gPath + base;\n\n    unsigned int d[RPT][RPT];\n    unsigned int p[RPT][RPT];\n#pragma unroll\n    for (int a = 0; a < RPT; ++a) {\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int b = 0; b < RPT; ++b) {\n            const int idx = (ty + 16 * b) * TILE + (tx + 16 * a);\n            d[a][b] = D[idx];\n            p[a][b] = Pa[idx];\n        }\n    }\n    __syncthreads();\n\n    for (int kp = 0; kp < kmax; ++kp) {\n        unsigned int cv[RPT];\n        unsigned int rv[RPT];\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int a = 0; a < RPT; ++a) cv[a] = sCol[kp * TILE + tx + 16 * a];\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int b = 0; b < RPT; ++b) rv[b] = sRow[kp * TILE + ty + 16 * b];\n\n        const unsigned int kg = static_cast<unsigned int>(kBase + kp);\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int a = 0; a < RPT; ++a) {\n#pragma unroll\n            for (int b = 0; b < RPT; ++b) {\n                const unsigned int nd = cv[a] + rv[b];\n                if (nd < d[a][b]) {\n                    d[a][b] = nd;\n                    p[a][b] = kg;\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n#pragma unroll\n    for (int a = 0; a < RPT; ++a) {\n#pragma unroll\n        for (int b = 0; b < RPT; ++b) {\n            const int idx = (ty + 16 * b) * TILE + (tx + 16 * a);\n            D[idx] = d[a][b];\n            Pa[idx] = p[a][b];\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n// Host side\n// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n// Number of indices in [0, numTiles) congruent to `index` modulo `dim`.\nstatic inline int localCount(const int numTiles, const int index, const int dim) {\n    return numTiles > index ? (numTiles - index - 1) / dim + 1 : 0;\n}\n\nstruct Decomposition {\n    int P = 1, Q = 1;       // process grid: P process rows, Q process columns\n    int r = 0, c = 0;       // this rank's grid coordinates (rank = r*Q + c)\n    int NB = 0;             // tiles per matrix dimension\n    int NLI = 0, NLJ = 0;   // locally owned tile rows / tile columns\n    MPI_Comm rowComm = MPI_COMM_NULL;  // ranks sharing r; rank index equals c\n    MPI_Comm colComm = MPI_COMM_NULL;  // ranks sharing c; rank index equals r\n};\n\nstatic Decomposition makeDecomposition(const int rank, const int size, const size_t n) {\n    Decomposition d;\n    int dims[2] = {0, 0};\n    MPI_Dims_create(size, 2, dims);\n    d.P = dims[0];\n    d.Q = dims[1];\n    d.r = rank / d.Q;\n    d.c = rank % d.Q;\n    d.NB = static_cast<int>((n + TILE - 1) / TILE);\n    d.NLI = localCount(d.NB, d.r, d.P);\n    d.NLJ = localCount(d.NB, d.c, d.Q);\n    MPI_Comm_split(MPI_COMM_WORLD, d.r, d.c, &d.rowComm);\n    MPI_Comm_split(MPI_COMM_WORLD, d.c, d.r, &d.colComm);\n    return d;\n}\n\nstatic void selectDevice() {\n    int numDevices = 0;\n    CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetDeviceCount(&numDevices));\n    if (numDevices == 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"No CUDA devices available\\n\");\n        MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);\n    }\n    MPI_Comm shm;\n    MPI_Comm_split_type(MPI_COMM_WORLD, MPI_COMM_TYPE_SHARED, 0, MPI_INFO_NULL, &shm);\n    int localRank = 0;\n    MPI_Comm_rank(shm, &localRank);\n    MPI_Comm_free(&shm);\n    CUDA_CHECK(cudaSetDevice(localRank % numDevices));\n}\n\n// Fills this rank's tiles. The random values are identical to the original\n// initializeDistanceMatrix(): rand_r (seed 42) consumed in storage order\n// (element (x,y) at index y*n + x). The path matrix is identical to the original\n// initializePathMatrix(), which yields path(x,y) = y.\nstatic void initializeLocalTiles(const Decomposition& d, const size_t n,\n                                 unsigned int* dist, unsigned int* path) {\n    const long long numLocal = static_cast<long long>(d.NLI) * d.NLJ;\n\n#pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)\n    for (long long t = 0; t < numLocal; ++t) {\n        const int li = static_cast<int>(t / d.NLJ);\n        const int lj = static_cast<int>(t % d.NLJ);\n        const size_t I = static_cast<size_t>(d.r + li * d.P);\n        const size_t J = static_cast<size_t>(d.c + lj * d.Q);\n        unsigned int* D = dist + static_cast<size_t>(t) * TT;\n        unsigned int* Pa = path + static_cast<size_t>(t) * TT;\n        for (int yl = 0; yl < TILE; ++yl) {\n            for (int xl = 0; xl < TILE; ++xl) {\n                const size_t x = I * TILE + xl;\n                const size_t y = J * TILE + yl;\n                D[yl * TILE + xl] = (x == y) ? 0u : INF;  // padding stays INF\n                Pa[yl * TILE + xl] = static_cast<unsigned int>(y);\n            }\n        }\n    }\n\n    unsigned int seed = 42;\n    const unsigned int rangeMin = 1;\n    const unsigned int rangeMax = MAX_DISTANCE;\n    const double range = static_cast<double>(rangeMax - rangeMin) + 1.0;\n\n    // Serial by necessity: the rand_r stream must be consumed in storage order.\n    for (size_t y = 0; y < n; ++y) {\n        const int J = static_cast<int>(y / TILE);\n        const int yl = static_cast<int>(y % TILE);\n        const bool colOwned = (J % d.Q) == d.c;\n        const int lj = J / d.Q;\n        for (size_t x = 0; x < n; ++x) {\n            const unsigned int value =\n                rangeMin + (unsigned int)(range * rand_r(&seed) / (double)RAND_MAX);\n            const int I = static_cast<int>(x / TILE);\n            if (colOwned && (I % d.P) == d.r) {\n                const int li = I / d.P;\n                const size_t t = static_cast<size_t>(li) * d.NLJ + lj;\n                dist[t * TT + yl * TILE + static_cast<int>(x % TILE)] = (x == y) ? 0u : value;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n}\n\n// Runs the blocked Floyd-Warshall over all tiles. Device-resident tiles are\n// updated in place; the snapshot buffers are exchanged through pinned host memory.\nstatic void runBlockedFloydWarshall(const Decomposition& d, const size_t n,\n                                    unsigned int* dDist, unsigned int* dPath,\n                                    unsigned int* dDiagSnap, unsigned int* dColSnap,\n                                    unsigned int* dRowSnap, unsigned int* hDiagSnap,\n                                    unsigned int* hColSnap, unsigned int* hRowSnap) {\n    const size_t colElems = static_cast<size_t>(d.NLI) * TT;\n    const size_t rowElems = static_cast<size_t>(d.NLJ) * TT;\n    const size_t diagBytes = 2 * TT * sizeof(unsigned int);\n\n    for (int K = 0; K < d.NB; ++K) {\n        const int kBase = K * TILE;\n        const int kmax = static_cast<int>(std::min<size_t>(TILE, n - static_cast<size_t>(kBase)));\n        const bool ownsRow = (K % d.P) == d.r;  // this rank holds tile row K\n        const bool ownsCol = (K % d.Q) == d.c;  // this rank holds tile column K\n        const bool ownsDiag = ownsRow && ownsCol;\n        const int diagRoot = (K % d.P) * d.Q + (K % d.Q);\n\n        // 1. Pivot tile (K,K): sequential phases, emit pivot row/column snapshots.\n        if (ownsDiag) {\n            const size_t off = (static_cast<size_t>(K / d.P) * d.NLJ + (K / d.Q)) * TT;\n            panelKernel<PANEL_DIAG><<<1, THREADS>>>(dDist + off, dPath + off, 0, 0, 1, K, kBase,\n                                                    kmax, nullptr, dDiagSnap);\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(hDiagSnap, dDiagSnap, diagBytes, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));\n        }\n        MPI_Bcast(hDiagSnap, 2 * TT, MPI_UNSIGNED, diagRoot, MPI_COMM_WORLD);\n        if (!ownsDiag) {\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dDiagSnap, hDiagSnap, diagBytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));\n        }\n\n        // 2. Column panel (I,K) and row panel (K,J), in parallel across owners.\n        if (ownsCol && d.NLI > 0) {\n            panelKernel<PANEL_COL><<<d.NLI, THREADS>>>(\n                dDist + static_cast<size_t>(K / d.Q) * TT, dPath + static_cast<size_t>(K / d.Q) * TT,\n                static_cast<size_t>(d.NLJ) * TT, d.r, d.P, K, kBase, kmax, dDiagSnap, dColSnap);\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());\n        }\n        if (ownsRow && d.NLJ > 0) {\n            const size_t off = static_cast<size_t>(K / d.P) * d.NLJ * TT;\n            panelKernel<PANEL_ROW><<<d.NLJ, THREADS>>>(dDist + off, dPath + off, TT, d.c, d.Q, K,\n                                                       kBase, kmax, dDiagSnap + TT, dRowSnap);\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());\n        }\n\n        // 3. Share the panel snapshots: column panels along process rows,\n        //    row panels along process columns.\n        if (ownsCol && colElems > 0) {\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(hColSnap, dColSnap, colElems * sizeof(unsigned int),\n                                  cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));\n        }\n        MPI_Bcast(hColSnap, static_cast<int>(colElems), MPI_UNSIGNED, K % d.Q, d.rowComm);\n        if (!ownsCol && colElems > 0) {\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dColSnap, hColSnap, colElems * sizeof(unsigned int),\n                                  cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));\n        }\n\n        if (ownsRow && rowElems > 0) {\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(hRowSnap, dRowSnap, rowElems * sizeof(unsigned int),\n                                  cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost));\n        }\n        MPI_Bcast(hRowSnap, static_cast<int>(rowElems), MPI_UNSIGNED, K % d.P, d.colComm);\n        if (!ownsRow && rowElems > 0) {\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dRowSnap, hRowSnap, rowElems * sizeof(unsigned int),\n                                  cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));\n        }\n\n        // 4. All remaining local tiles, fused over the kmax pivots of block K.\n        if (d.NLI > 0 && d.NLJ > 0) {\n            updateKernel<<<dim3(d.NLJ, d.NLI), THREADS>>>(dDist, dPath, d.NLJ, d.r, d.c, d.P, d.Q,\n                                                          K, kBase, kmax, dColSnap, dRowSnap);\n            CUDA_CHECK(cudaGetLastError());\n        }\n    }\n    CUDA_CHECK(cudaDeviceSynchronize());\n}\n\n// Places the tiles of rank (rr,cc) (packed as [tile][yl][xl]) into the full\n// matrix stored in the original layout (element (x,y) at y*n + x).\nstatic void scatterTiles(const unsigned int* src, const int rr, const int cc, const Decomposition& d,\n                         const size_t n, std::vector<unsigned int>& out) {\n    const int NLI = localCount(d.NB, rr, d.P);\n    const int NLJ = localCount(d.NB, cc, d.Q);\n    const long long numLocal = static_cast<long long>(NLI) * NLJ;\n\n#pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)\n    for (long long t = 0; {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793141784393,"sessionID":"ses_e807c23a9ffecLzhcZkkw485d1","part":{"id":"prt_17f940d570013O2muT4Au2bnqr","messageID":"msg_17f9406c4001xq6tBRnaut6WK5","sessionID":"ses_e807c23a9ffecLzhcZkkw485d1","type":"reasoning","text":"The timing numbers look suspicious — np=2 and np=1 matching exactly at 52ms seems odd, and np=4 scaling worse than np=2 at larger sizes suggests the multi-GPU setup isn't distributing properly. I suspect the rank-to-GPU assignment logic with oversubscribe might be putting multiple ranks on the same device.\n\nChecking the throughput math: for n=8192, the computed updates-per-second rate seems plausible for a single RTX 3090's CUDA core count, so the raw single-GPU numbers check out even if impressive. But scaling from 1 to 4 GPUs barely helps, meaning per-block synchronization overhead (MPI broadcasts, memory copies) is eating most of the theoretical speedup since each block's compute time is small relative to coordination costs.\n\nWorking out the S4 kernel's update count: total updates across all tiles scale as n²·B, giving roughly 4.3e9 updates spread over all GPUs, so about 1.07e9 per GPU.\n\nAt throughput 1.8e12/s that's 0.6ms per block, so 128 blocks should total 77ms at np=4, yet measured time is 297ms—implying ~1.7ms overhead per block from panel kernels or MPI. Checking np=1, the numbers line up almost exactly with pure compute time (2.35ms per block vs 2.4ms predicted), meaning at single GPU there's no overhead and the S4 kernel itself is the bottleneck.\n\nBut that raises a puzzle: with np=4 each GPU should only handle a quarter of the tiles (4096 of 16384), so the runtime should drop proportionally unless something is wrong—maybe the device assignment via MPI_COMM_TYPE_SHARED isn't actually spreading ranks across different GPUs. I want to verify this by checking nvidia-smi during a run or adding a debug print of the assigned device per rank, and also consider whether CPU-side initialization (the random number generation loop) is adding non-trivial overhead per rank.\n\nI'll quickly check this by running nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps while the job executes.\n\n","time":{"start":1793141771607,"end":1793141784344},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793142009736,"sessionID":"ses_e807c23a9ffecLzhcZkkw485d1","part":{"id":"prt_17f96e59a001kiGuz0uvS6h1Gz","messageID":"msg_17f96db82001a0nMvF1E9DFKZa","sessionID":"ses_e807c23a9ffecLzhcZkkw485d1","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm calculating that the updateKernel averages 1.73ms across 256 blocks per rank, totaling about 443ms of kernel time per GPU out of the 1.4s overall run time.\n\nThe rest of the time seems tied up in memcpy operations — summing to ~425ms per rank across ranks, with D2H colSnap copies averaging 494us for 1MB transfers, which works out to only ~2GB/s. That's surprisingly slow for pinned memory allocated via cudaHostAlloc, which should hit 10+GB/s, so something's throttling these transfers, possibly serialization. Adding kernel time, memcpy time, and MPI broadcast waits roughly accounts for the full runtime, though I want to check why updateKernel timing differs so much between single-GPU and multi-GPU runs by recomputing the tile counts and update throughput at np=1.\n\nWorking through the math: at n=16384, each block handles 65536 tiles of 262144 updates each, giving 1.7e10 updates per block and 4.4e12 total across 256 blocks, matching n³ scaling as expected. At np=4, each GPU does a quarter of that work in 1.73ms per block, which translates to ~2.5e12 updates/s — and scaling this back to np=1 predicts 2065ms, matching the measured value, so the kernel itself is performing at its ideal rate on both configurations. This means the kernel isn't the bottleneck at np=4: with kernel time at 0.44s matching the ideal compute time, the remaining ~1s of runtime is being consumed by memcpy overhead (420ms) and MPI/panel kernel overhead (~550ms). I'm now thinking about how to reduce memcpy overhead, starting with examining colSnap transfer sizes per rank at n=16384.\n\nLooking at the P=2,Q=2 case specifically, I calculate roughly 2MB per D2H/H2D copy, which at expected PCIe bandwidth should only take a fraction of a millisecond, but measured timings show much higher overhead than the math predicts — suggesting either bandwidth isn't being fully utilized or there's some other cost involved, even though pinned memory is already being used. For reduction strategies, I rule out shrinking the colSnap data itself since the full snapshot is needed for this algorithm's correctness, and I'm now considering whether CUDA-aware MPI could let us broadcast device buffers directly and skip the D2H/H2D staging entirely — though I'm wary since that feature isn't guaranteed to be available or reliable on this cluster.\n\nMy more promising idea is pipelining: lookahead by splitting the S4 computation so the tiles needed for the next pivot block (K+1) are computed first on one stream, while the remaining bulk of S4 for the current block runs concurrently on a second stream. This way the heavy communication and copy overhead for block K+1 can overlap with leftover computation from block K, potentially hiding nearly all the ~0.4s of comm/copy cost behind the ~0.44s kernel time and cutting the np=4 runtime from 1.41s down toward something like 0.6s. I'm sketching out how to implement this with two CUDA streams — a main stream carrying the critical path (panel plus communication) and a bulk stream handling the non-critical S4 tiles, where the critical tiles are identified as those sharing the row or column index of the next pivot.\n\nBut I realize the critical S4 for K+1 can touch tiles still being processed by bulk(K) on streamBulk, so I need to insert an event wait before launching that critical step, making streamMain pause until streamBulk catches up. Ideally bulk(K) finishes during the diag/panel/comm phase of K+1 so this wait costs nothing, meaning each iteration's critical S4 must first wait on the previous iteration's bulk-done event before proceeding.\n\nSo the ordering works: launch bulk(K-1) right after crit(K-1), let it overlap with diag(K)/comm(K)/panel(K), then have crit(K) wait on bulk(K-1)'s completion event before proceeding. But now I'm spotting a hazard: the bulk S4 kernel reads the snapshot buffers from block K-1 while the next block's panel kernels would overwrite those same snapshot buffers, so I need double-buffering to avoid a race there.\n\nDouble-buffering the col/row snapshot buffers by K parity fixes this, and I'm checking that diagSnap doesn't need the same treatment since it's only read by panel(K) and rewritten later in-order on the same stream. I'm also working out the event synchronization so the bulk stream waits for the snapshot H2D transfer on the main stream before launching, and double-checking the D2H copy ordering for the snapshot owner.\n\nI'm distinguishing critical versus bulk tiles by having the update kernel take a mode parameter and early-exit based on whether a tile touches row/column K+1, so a single kernel covers both passes with the full grid dimensions.\n\nTiming-wise, I estimate each block is dominated by the bulk kernel (~1.73ms) running concurrently with communication and panel work (~1ms), making the critical update tiny by comparison, so overall runtime for np=4 lands around 0.45-0.5s. I also note that async memcopies for snapshots use DMA engines and won't block the concurrent kernels, unlike a synchronous copy on the default stream which would stall everything.\n\nI'm settling on using an explicit non-blocking streamMain for all launches and copies, syncing it right before the MPI exchange step, since the legacy default stream only implicitly syncs with blocking streams and ours are non-blocking. I'm double-checking that each snapshot copy correctly waits on its producing kernel, and that syncing streamMain only waits on the critical-path kernels there, not the separate bulk stream.\n\nFor dependencies between streams, I'm weighing whether to use CUDA events (bulkDone recorded after bulk(K-1), snapReady after the snapshot H2D) versus just relying on host-side synchronization, since syncing streamMain after each H2D copy already guarantees ordering before bulk(K) is enqueued without needing an event. The remaining question is how crit(K) should wait for bulk(K-1) — doing a full host-side cudaStreamSynchronize(streamBulk) would stall the host unnecessarily, so an event-based wait seems better there.\n\nWorking through the full per-iteration order on the host: diag(K), then D2H/bcast/H2D with a sync, then COL/ROW(K) with the same pattern, then crit(K) which needs to wait on bulkDone via cudaStreamWaitEvent so the host doesn't block, then bulk(K) on streamBulk which stays correctly ordered since it's in-order with bulk(K-1) and reads snapshots that are already host-synced from streamMain — I'm confirming there's no tile overlap hazard between crit(K) and bulk(K) since their index ranges are disjoint.\n\nI'm now verifying that diag/panel(K+1) only ever reads tiles that were written by crit(K), never by bulk(K), so the in-order execution within streamMain is sufficient without extra synchronization there. Then I check the double-buffered snapshot scheme: iteration K+2 reuses buffer (K&1), and since it only writes that buffer after step 4's wait on bulkDone(K+1) (which itself is ordered after bulk(K) completes), the buffer reuse should be safe — I'm tracing through whether the COL/ROW write in iteration K+2 could race ahead of that wait.\n\nI also confirm the single-buffer dDiagSnap is only ever touched by streamMain, so there's no cross-stream hazard there, and that host-side pinned staging buffers for MPI are safe since those transfers are synchronous and don't overlap GPU execution. Finally I'm checking that the closing synchronizations on both streams and the MPI broadcast ordering hold up correctly.\n\nTiming-wise, at np=4 the per-block cost is roughly bounded by the larger of the bulk kernel and the panel communication (~1.7ms vs ~1ms), giving an estimated ~0.45s total runtime dominated by kernel work; at np=1 there's no communication so it's purely kernel-bound as before. Running the critical and bulk kernels concurrently shouldn't hurt efficiency much since total SM work stays the same, though I note the critical kernel only touches a couple of small boundary tiles.\n\nI'm now thinking about whether the S4 kernel's throughput could be improved — looking at occupancy limits from shared memory usage (32KB per block limiting to ~3 blocks per SM, roughly 50% occupancy) and considering whether reducing shared memory footprint, perhaps by broadcasting pivot values differently, could help, though I'll set that optimization aside for now.\n\nI'm now working out how to implement stream-based lookahead: adding a mode parameter to the update kernel to distinguish critical versus bulk tile updates, double-buffering the snapshot buffers, and setting up separate CUDA streams (main and bulk) with an event to synchronize them, replacing synchronous memcpys with async ones on the main stream. I also need to handle edge cases — guarding against zero-size grid launches when there are no bulk tiles, and skipping the critical kernel launch (and its associated wait) when K+1 reaches the last block since there's nothing for it to update.\n\nI'm reorganizing the per-iteration loop so diagonal, row/column, and snapshot work happen on the main stream, followed by a critical update that waits on the previous iteration's bulk-done event (a no-op the first time since the event hasn't been recorded yet), then launching the bulk update on the separate stream and recording its completion event for the next iteration to wait on.\n\nChecking the ordering more carefully, the snapshot buffer reuse is safe since the critical step at iteration K always waits for the prior bulk to finish before the next column/row snapshot overwrites the same double-buffer slot, and GPU stream ordering guarantees the host-to-device and device-to-host copies stay sequenced correctly even when the critical step is skipped near the last tile.\n\nI'm confirming bulk(K+1) safely reads the H2D snapshots since the host synchronizes streamMain before launching it, so cross-stream ordering holds even without an explicit event wait. I'm also checking that crit(K) correctly waits on bulk(K-1) since their tile sets overlap on row/col K+1, and now tracing whether panel kernels at step K could conflict with bulk(K-1)'s tile exclusion criteria.\n\nWriting the kernel's mode-check logic...\n\nI'm verifying the diagonal tile dependencies line up correctly with the critical phase ordering, then sketching helper functions for synchronized copies and stream/event creation with non-blocking flags and disabled timing.\n\nThe H2D transfer stays off the critical path since it overlaps with the bulk kernel on a separate stream, so I'm ready to write the actual code changes for the blocked Floyd-Warshall function, the update kernel, and the double-buffer/stream allocation in main.\n\n","time":{"start":1793141958042,"end":1793142009693},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

The panel factorization and exchange for block K can proceed once the previous panel update finished, so that latency gets hidden behind the big bulk computation, and only the dependency between panel/communication and the trailing update actually has to wait.\n\nSince bulk_K only touches tiles disjoint from P_K ∪ N_K, it just needs the snapshots, not N_K's completion — so it can start right after bulk_{K-1} finishes and comm K lands, independent of main_K's progress.\n\nThe N_K update needs bulk_{K-1} done, and main_{K+1}'s panel needs N_K done plus comm K+1 (which depends on diag K+1, itself inside N_K).
